meaning: 1) An action is completely finished, done all the way ("... up, ... off, finish ...ing"); 2) something happened that the speaker did not want and that cannot be undone, with a tone of regret, remorse, or frustration ("accidentally ...", "ended up ...ing").
connection: Verb te-form + しまう (colloquial contraction: 〜ちゃう／〜じゃう)
usage: It attaches to the verb te-form, and しまう itself conjugates as a godan verb: てしまった, てしまいます, てしまおう, てしまえば, てしまって.
Colloquial contractions: てしまう→ちゃう, でしまう→じゃう; てしまった→ちゃった／じゃった, てしまいます→ちゃいます. Kansai dialect also has forms like 〜てもうた.

The "completion" meaning often goes with words like 全部・もう・早く, and the volitional 〜てしまおう is common for "let's just get it all done". The "regret" meaning usually uses the past 〜てしまった, often with the speaker as subject.
With non-volitional verbs (忘れる, 壊れる, 遅れる, etc.) it almost always means regret; with volitional verbs either meaning is possible, and context decides.
Formal writing usually uses the full form 〜てしまう; ちゃう／じゃう are colloquial and unsuitable for formal texts or formal situations with superiors.
scenarios: Apologizing or expressing regret to someone: 「約束の時間に遅れてしまって、すみません。」
Casual complaining among friends: 「またケーキ食べちゃった。」
Deciding to just get something done: 「今日中にレポートを書いてしまおう。」
In narration, conveying an unexpected or irreversible result: 「彼はそのまま国へ帰ってしまった。」
etymology: しまう is written 「仕舞う」 in kanji, originally meaning "to end, to settle; to put away, to tidy up", and is cognate with the noun 「仕舞い（しまい）」 "end, finish" (as in 「おしまい」 "it's over"). From "settling a matter" it came to mean "completing an action fully", and from "the matter is settled and can't be undone" it gained its tone of regret. The colloquial ちゃう developed from てしまう via ちまう; 〜ちまう is already found in colloquial speech of the Edo to Meiji periods.
examples: I finished all my homework.
I (accidentally) left my umbrella on the train.
I broke an important plate.
Let's wait until the child finishes reading the book.
After taking the medicine, I fell asleep right away.

similar.title: 〜ておく
similar.explanation: Both can mean "get something done", but 〜ておく focuses on preparing in advance for later, while 〜てしまう focuses on finishing it off or on regret. 「ビールを冷やしておく」 is chilling beer ahead of a party; 「ビールを全部飲んでしまった」 is having drunk it all (possibly with regret).

similar.title: 〜終わる
similar.explanation: Verb masu-stem + 終わる simply states that an action ends in time (読み終わる = finish reading), with no regret or remorse, and it can't follow non-volitional verbs. 〜てしまう can carry the speaker's subjective evaluation.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: 〜てしまっている expresses "a state of having (undesirably) already been completed continues", as in 「もう出発してしまっている」. Plain 〜ている only expresses progress or a resulting state, without the sense of completeness or regret.

meaning: 1) Doing something in advance to prepare for the future ("do ... ahead of time"); 2) keeping a state as it is, leaving it alone ("leave ... as is"); 3) doing something for the time being ("do ... for now").
connection: Verb te-form + おく (colloquial contraction: 〜とく／〜どく)
usage: おく conjugates as a godan verb: ておいた, ておきます, ておこう, ておいて, ておけば, ておかないと.
Colloquial contractions: ておく→とく, でおく→どく; ておいて→といて, ておいた→といた, ておこう→とこう. E.g. 「買っとく」, 「読んどいて」.
The "preparation" meaning is most common and often pairs with 前に・までに・あらかじめ. The "leave as is" meaning often uses 〜ておいてください／〜ておく to mean "keep it as it is, don't touch it", as in 「窓は開けておいてください」.
To ask someone, use 〜ておいてください／〜ておいてくれる？; to state your own intention, use 〜ておきます, which sounds proactive and considerate.
It can be written 「〜て置く」 with kanji, but as an auxiliary verb in modern writing it is usually written in kana.
scenarios: Preparing before a trip, exam, or meeting: 「旅行の前にホテルを予約しておきます。」
Assigning tasks at work: 「明日までに資料をコピーしておいてください。」
Casual speech among friends: 「ビール冷やしとくね。」
Keeping things as they are: 「エアコンはつけておいていいよ。」
etymology: おく is written 「置く」, originally meaning "to put, to place, to set down". Putting something somewhere and leaving it there extended to "keeping a certain state for later use", so 〜ておく developed both the "advance preparation" and "leave as is" uses. In speech, the two vowels of te-o run together, the o drops, and 〜とく results.
examples: I booked a hotel before the trip.
Please put it back where it was after using it.
It's fine to leave the window open.
I'll have this book read by tomorrow.
Let's buy the drinks before the party.

similar.title: 〜てある
similar.explanation: 〜てある describes "the state left after someone did something for a purpose", focusing on the resulting state, and the subject is often marked with が (「ビールが冷やしてある」); 〜ておく focuses on the act of preparing itself (「ビールを冷やしておく」).

similar.title: 〜てしまう
similar.explanation: 〜てしまう stresses finishing off or regret; 〜ておく stresses preparing for later. 「食べておく」 is eating something now so you won't be hungry later; 「食べてしまう」 is eating it all up.

similar.title: 〜っぱなし
similar.explanation: 〜っぱなし means "leaving something in a state without dealing with it", with a critical nuance (「電気をつけっぱなしにする」); the "leave as is" of 〜ておく is usually intentional and not critical.

meaning: Try doing something and see how it turns out ("try ...ing", "... and see").
connection: Verb te-form + みる
usage: みる conjugates as an ichidan verb: てみた, てみます, てみよう, てみたい, てみて, てみれば, てみない？
As an auxiliary verb it is generally written in kana as 「みる」, not 「見る」; when written 「見る」 it is usually the content verb "to see".
Common combinations: 〜てみたい (I'd like to try), 〜てみてください (please try), 〜てみませんか (would you like to try?), 〜てみたら (when I tried ..., I found ... / why don't you try ...).
〜てみたら／〜てみると is often followed by an unexpected discovery: 「食べてみたら、おいしかった。」
Don't confuse it with 〜てみせる, which means "show someone how to do it" or "I'll definitely do it".
scenarios: Making a suggestion: 「この服、着てみてください。」
Expressing a wish: 「一度富士山に登ってみたいです。」
Describing an experience and discovery: 「日本料理を作ってみたら、意外と簡単だった。」
Inviting someone: 「一緒にやってみませんか。」
etymology: みる is 「見る」 (to see). "Do it and then see what happens" — the meaning shifted from "see" to "try", a typical example in Japanese of a content verb becoming grammaticalized as an auxiliary verb. English shows a similar link between seeing and trying: "try it and see", "let's see if it fits".
examples: May I try these shoes on?
I'd like to visit Hokkaido at least once.
I tried eating at the new restaurant, and it was really good.
Let's look up words we don't know in the dictionary.
I tried writing a letter in Japanese.

similar.title: 〜ようとする
similar.explanation: 〜ようとする means "attempt to, be about to"; the action often isn't realized or doesn't succeed (「ドアを開けようとしたが、開かなかった」). 〜てみる means you actually did it to see the result.

similar.title: 〜てみせる
similar.explanation: 〜てみせる means "show someone by doing" or "(be determined to) definitely do" (「必ず合格してみせる」); it has nothing to do with trying.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: 〜たい simply means wanting to do something; 〜てみたい means "want to give it a try", usually about something new you haven't done before, and sounds lighter and softer.

meaning: Indicates that someone intentionally did an action and its result remains ("has been ...ed", "is ...ed"), often implying it was done for some purpose.
connection: Transitive verb te-form + ある
usage: In principle it follows transitive verbs (書く, 置く, 貼る, 並べる, 予約する, etc.) and expresses the persistence of an action's result; for the resulting state of intransitive verbs use 〜ている (窓が開いている).
The object often becomes the subject with 「が」: 「黒板に字が書いてある」; when stressing preparation, 「を」 can be kept: 「ホテルを予約してある」.
The agent (who did it) usually isn't mentioned; the focus is on "this is the state now".
Conjugation: てあります, てあった, てあって; the negative is usually 〜ていない or 〜てない, not 〜てあらない.
Often paired with 〜ておく: once the preparation with 〜ておく is done, the result is 〜てある.
scenarios: Describing a room or the way a scene is set up: 「テーブルの上に花が飾ってあります。」
Explaining the content of notices or writing: 「ここに名前が書いてあります。」
Confirming preparations: 「もう切符は買ってあるから、大丈夫。」
Instructions and signboards: 「入口に地図が貼ってある。」
etymology: ある is 「有る／在る」, expressing the existence of inanimate things. "The result of a completed action exists there", so transitive te-form + ある expresses the persistence of a human-made result. Classical Japanese already had a similar use of 〜てあり, and the perfective auxiliary 〜たり itself later arose from the fusion of 「て＋あり」.
examples: Today's schedule is written on the blackboard.
There's a calendar put up on the wall.
The hotel is already booked, so please don't worry.
There was beer chilling in the fridge.
Old books are lined up on the bookshelf.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: Intransitive verb + ている only describes a state (「窓が開いている」 = the window is open, regardless of why); transitive verb + てある implies someone did it on purpose (「窓が開けてある」 = someone deliberately opened the window).

similar.title: 〜ておく
similar.explanation: 〜ておく focuses on the act of preparing in advance; 〜てある focuses on the state after the preparation is done. 「予約しておく」→「予約してある」.

meaning: Expresses a gradual change in ability, habit, or state: from not being able to do something to being able to, or from not doing it to starting to do it ("come to ...", "start ...ing", "become able to ...").
connection: Verb dictionary form / potential form + ようになる; verb nai-form + ようになる (〜なくなる is also common)
usage: With potential verbs it expresses gaining an ability: 「泳げるようになった」, 「漢字が読めるようになった」.
With ordinary verbs it expresses a change in habits or behavior: 「毎朝ジョギングするようになった」.
The past 〜ようになった is common, indicating that the change has happened; 〜ようになりたい expresses a hope.
For a negative change, 〜なくなる is more natural (「食べなくなった」); 〜ないようになる is possible but sounds stiffer.
Changes in nouns and adjectives don't use this pattern; use noun + になる and adjective く + なる instead (「先生になる」, 「暑くなる」).
scenarios: Talking about learning progress: 「日本語のニュースがわかるようになりました。」
Talking about changed habits: 「日本に来てから、納豆を食べるようになった。」
Talking about social change: 「最近は、スマホで買い物ができるようになった。」
Talking about a child growing up: 「娘は一人で服が着られるようになった。」
etymology: 「よう」 is written 「様」, originally meaning "appearance, state, manner"; 「に」 marks the result of a change, and 「なる」 means "to become". Literally, "to become the state of ...". As a formal noun in modern Japanese, 「様」 is usually written in kana.
examples: By practicing every day, I've become able to play the piano.
Since coming to Japan, I've started eating sashimi.
Once I put on glasses, I could see the writing on the blackboard clearly.
I want to be able to speak Japanese soon.

similar.title: 〜ようにする
similar.explanation: 〜ようにする expresses the subject's conscious effort (「毎日運動するようにしている」); 〜ようになる expresses a change that happens naturally as a result.

similar.title: 〜ことになる
similar.explanation: 〜ことになる expresses an arrangement or decision (not made by oneself) (「転勤することになった」); it has nothing to do with gradual changes in ability or habit.

similar.title: 〜くなる／〜になる
similar.explanation: Changes in adjectives and nouns use 高くなる, 静かになる, 医者になる; only changes in verbs use 〜ようになる.

meaning: 1) Making a conscious effort to do (or not do) something; 2) 〜ようにしている expresses a long-standing habit ("try to ..., make a point of ...").
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ようにする
usage: 〜ようにする: resolving to do something from now on; 〜ようにしている: a habit already formed and kept up.
The negative is 〜ないようにする: 「遅刻しないようにします」 (I'll make sure not to be late).
When asking others, 〜ようにしてください is softer than 〜てください and stresses "please make sure to": 「明日は8時に来るようにしてください」.
The final する conjugates normally: ようにした, ようにします, ようにしよう, ようにして.
The subject is usually a person acting with intention; the preceding verb can be volitional or potential (「見えるようにする」 = make it visible).
scenarios: Talking about healthy habits: 「毎日野菜を食べるようにしています。」
Instructions at work: 「会議には遅れないようにしてください。」
Reflecting on yourself or making a resolution: 「これからはもっと早く寝るようにします。」
Explaining arrangements: 「子どもにも見えるように、字を大きくするようにした。」
etymology: 「よう（様）」 means "appearance, state", and 「にする」 means "to make it into". Literally, "to make (one's behavior) into the state of ...", from which it came to mean "make an effort to, make sure to".
examples: For my health, I make a point of walking every day.
From tomorrow, I'll try to get up earlier.
Please make sure you aren't late for class.
Let's try not to look at our phones before bed.

similar.title: 〜ようになる
similar.explanation: 〜ようになる is a natural change; 〜ようにする is a deliberate effort. 「話せるようになった」 means your ability improved; 「話すようにしている」 means you keep making a point of speaking.

similar.title: 〜ことにする
similar.explanation: 〜ことにする expresses a one-time decision (「タバコをやめることにした」); 〜ようにする expresses ongoing effort and care, not necessarily achieved 100%.

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: In 「忘れないようにメモする」, ように expresses purpose and is followed by another action; in 〜ようにする, ように and する form a single unit.

meaning: Expresses that the speaker thinks something is possible, with low certainty (about 50% or less): "may, might, perhaps, maybe".
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + かもしれない; na-adjective stem / noun + かもしれない (without だ)
usage: It follows the plain form, but nouns and na-adjectives don't take だ: 「雨かもしれない」, 「暇かもしれない」 (✕雨だかもしれない).
Polite: かもしれません; guess about the past: 〜たかもしれない; "it might have been the case (back then)": 〜かもしれなかった.
In casual speech it is often shortened to 〜かも: 「明日、雨かも。」, 「それ、いいかもね。」
Often paired with もしかしたら／もしかすると／ひょっとしたら to lower certainty even further.
Can be used to express your opinion indirectly: 「ちょっと難しいかもしれませんね。」 (really a polite "no").
scenarios: Uncertain forecasts about weather or plans: 「午後から雨が降るかもしれません。」
Expressing an opinion tactfully: 「その計画は少し無理かもしれません。」
A casual guess among friends: 「あの人、先生かも。」
Pointing out a risk: 「遅れるかもしれないから、早めに出よう。」
etymology: Made of the question particle 「か」 + the particle 「も」 + 「知れない」 (cannot be known). Literally, "whether it is ... can't be known", i.e. "it may be ...". 「知れない」 can be written in kanji as 「かも知れない」, but today kana is more common. The casual shortening 〜かも has spread in the last few decades.
examples: It might rain from the afternoon.
He may have already gone home.
That person might be a teacher, you know.
This cake might be a little too sweet.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 〜はずだ is a fairly confident judgment based on reasoning or facts ("it should be ..."); 〜かもしれない has low certainty and only says the possibility exists.

similar.title: 〜だろう／〜でしょう
similar.explanation: 〜だろう expresses a fairly confident guess (70-80%); 〜かもしれない is much less certain, meaning only "that can't be ruled out".

similar.title: 〜に違いない
similar.explanation: 〜に違いない expresses strong conviction ("it must be ..."), far more certain than 〜かもしれない.

meaning: 1) A confident inference based on some grounds or reasoning ("should be ..., ought to ..."); 2) 〜はずだった expresses what should have happened but didn't; 3) a sudden realization: "no wonder ...".
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + はずだ; na-adjective + な + はずだ; noun + の + はずだ
usage: There must be grounds for the judgment: 「チケットは昨日送ったから、今日届くはずだ。」
Polite: はずです; before nouns: はずの〜; connective: はずなのに, はずで.
〜はずだった／〜はずでした means "was supposed to ... (but didn't)": 「3時に着くはずだったのに、遅れてしまった。」
There are two negative inferences: 〜ないはずだ (it shouldn't be ...) and 〜はずがない (there's no way ...); the latter is much stronger.
It cannot express your own intention or decision: ✕「明日行くはずです」 (to say "I plan to go", use 〜つもりだ／予定だ).
scenarios: Inferring from facts: 「鍵はかばんに入れたはずです。」
Confirming a schedule: 「会議は3時からのはずですが……。」
Expressing that things didn't go as expected: 「今日は晴れるはずだったのに。」
A sudden realization: 「彼は日本に10年住んでいたのか。日本語が上手なはずだ。」
etymology: 「はず」 is written 「筈」 in kanji. It originally referred to the notch at the end of an arrow that fits onto the bowstring (矢筈). The arrow's notch and the string "naturally have to fit together", which gave rise to the meaning "it stands to reason, it must be so". As a formal noun in modern Japanese it is usually written in kana.
examples: I sent the package yesterday, so it should arrive today.
He lived in Japan for ten years, so his Japanese must be good.
The train was supposed to arrive at nine, but it still hasn't come.
Today is Sunday, so the bank should be closed.

similar.title: 〜はずがない
similar.explanation: 〜はずがない is a strong denial, "there's absolutely no way ...", much stronger than 〜ないはずだ (it shouldn't be ...).

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: 〜かもしれない only says something is possible, with low certainty; 〜はずだ is based on solid grounds and is highly certain.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: Both can mean "no wonder", but 〜わけだ focuses on a conclusion following naturally from a premise or explaining a cause, while 〜はずだ focuses on being convinced because it matches expectations.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: 〜つもりだ expresses your own plans; 〜はずだ is an inference about objective facts and cannot describe your own plans.

meaning: 1) An intuitive judgment based on appearance ("looks ..., seems ..."); 2) with verbs, a sign or feeling that something is about to happen ("looks like it's about to ...").
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + そうだ; i-adjective (drop い) + そうだ (いい→よさそう, ない→なさそう); na-adjective stem + そうだ
usage: Conjugates like a na-adjective: そうな + noun (おいしそうなケーキ), そうに + verb (楽しそうに話す), そうです, そうだった.
Irregular forms: いい→よさそう, ない→なさそう, adjective negative 〜くない→〜くなさそう.
With verbs it means "about to ...": 「雨が降りそうだ」, 「シャツのボタンが取れそうだ」. Negative: 降りそうもない／降りそうにない.

Used only for your own judgment of what you see; it can't be used for facts obvious at a glance: ✕「このりんごは赤そうだ」. Qualities like "pretty" or "cute" that are apparent at a glance generally don't take it either (きれいそう).
Nouns cannot directly take the appearance そうだ (✕学生そうだ); use 〜らしい／〜みたいだ／〜っぽい instead.
scenarios: On seeing food: 「わあ、おいしそう！」
Describing someone's expression or state: 「彼女はうれしそうに笑った。」
Warning that something is about to happen: 「棚の上の箱が落ちそうですよ。」
Judging the weather: 「今にも雨が降りそうな空だ。」
etymology: 「そう」 comes from the kanji 「相」 (さう), originally meaning "outward appearance, look" (as in 人相 "physiognomy" and 手相 "palm lines"). From the medieval period onward 「〜さうなり」 was used as an auxiliary of appearance, which later became modern 〜そうだ. It has a different origin from the hearsay 〜そうだ, which is why the two attach differently.
examples: This cake looks delicious, doesn't it?
The sky looks like it could rain at any moment.
The children are playing happily.
It doesn't look like this job will be finished today.
He looked rather low on energy.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: The hearsay form follows the plain form: 「雨が降るそうだ」 = I hear it will rain; the appearance form follows the masu-stem: 「雨が降りそうだ」 = it looks like it's going to rain. The hearsay form has no そうな／そうに forms.

similar.title: 〜ようだ／〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: 〜ようだ is a judgment based on all kinds of information (not just visual) and can follow nouns; the appearance 〜そうだ relies more on the immediate visual impression and cannot directly follow nouns.

similar.title: 〜らしい
similar.explanation: 〜らしい mostly judges based on outside information or hearsay, with the speaker keeping some distance; 〜そうだ is the speaker's direct impression from what they see.

meaning: Passes on information heard from someone else, or read or seen in newspapers, on TV, etc. ("I hear that ..., apparently ..., they say ...").
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives / na-adjectives / nouns + そうだ (nouns・na-adjectives: 〜だそうだ)
usage: It follows the plain form, and nouns and na-adjectives take だ: 「雨だそうだ」, 「静かだそうだ」; the past tense can precede it too: 「行ったそうだ」.
It is only used in a few forms such as そうだ／そうです／そうで; it has no negative, no past (✕そうだった), and no そうな／そうに.
The source of information is often shown with 〜によると／〜の話では／〜では: 「天気予報によると、明日は雪だそうです。」
The speaker is only relaying information and takes no responsibility for its content; the tone is objective. It cannot be used for one's own experiences.
To distinguish it from the appearance 〜そうだ, look at what precedes it: 降るそうだ (hearsay) vs. 降りそうだ (appearance), 高いそうだ (hearsay) vs. 高そうだ (appearance).
scenarios: Relaying news or weather forecasts: 「ニュースによると、来月から電気代が上がるそうです。」
Passing on what someone said: 「田中さんは来週国へ帰るそうですよ。」
Sharing a review you heard: 「あの店のラーメンはとてもおいしいそうだ。」
Citing information in written language or reports: 「調査では、若者の読書時間が減っているそうである。」
etymology: The hearsay そうだ is generally thought to come from expressions like 「…と言う相（さう）だ」, meaning "it is said to be the case that ..."; from the Edo period onward it was used in the form 「〜さうだ」 to relay hearsay. Although it is written the same way as the appearance 〜そうだ, the two long ago split into separate auxiliaries, and they attach in completely different ways.
examples: According to the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow.
I hear Mr. Tanaka is getting married next month.
Apparently that restaurant is really expensive.
Apparently his father is a doctor.
I heard there was an accident near the station yesterday.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: The appearance form follows the masu-stem / adjective stem and means "looks ..."; the hearsay form follows the plain form and means "I hear ...". 「おいしそうだ」 = looks delicious; 「おいしいそうだ」 = I hear it's delicious.

similar.title: 〜らしい
similar.explanation: 〜らしい can also express hearsay, but it includes some of the speaker's own guesswork and the source is vaguer; 〜そうだ is a more direct, faithful report.

similar.title: 〜って／〜とのことだ
similar.explanation: In speech, 〜って is often used to relay information (「明日休みだって」); 〜とのことだ is a formal, written way of reporting, common in business.

meaning: 1) A guess or hearsay based on information heard or seen ("apparently ..., it seems ..., I hear ..."); 2) as a suffix after nouns, "like a typical ..., having the typical qualities of ..." (男らしい = manly).
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + らしい; na-adjective stem / noun + らしい (without だ)
usage: Conjugates as an i-adjective: らしかった, らしく, らしくない, らしいです.
In the guessing sense the basis is outside information (hearsay, visible signs), and the speaker keeps their distance and doesn't take full responsibility: 「彼は会社を辞めたらしい。」
In the suffix sense, "noun + らしい" means fitting the typical nature of that noun: 「今日は春らしい天気だ」, 「彼女らしくない」 (it's not like her).
In the guessing sense the negative comes before: 「来ないらしい」; in the suffix sense the negative is 〜らしくない.
Note that 素晴らしい, 新しい, 珍しい, いやらしい, etc. are independent adjectives; the らしい in them is not this grammar point.
scenarios: Passing on news you only half believe: 「あの店、来月閉まるらしいよ。」
Guessing from signs: 「道がぬれている。夜中に雨が降ったらしい。」
Judging whether someone or something lives up to its name: 「今日は本当に夏らしい一日だった。」
Commenting on someone casually: 「そんなことを言うなんて、君らしくないね。」
etymology: There are several theories about the origin of らしい. It is generally thought to be related to the old suffix 「〜らし」, meaning "appearance, being like" (as in 「男らし」), and to have gradually developed its use as an auxiliary of inference from the medieval to the early modern period. Classical Japanese also had a separate conjectural auxiliary 「らし」 (expressing an inference based on evidence), but scholars disagree on whether there is a direct line of descent between the two.
examples: The road is wet. It seems it rained during the night.
I hear that shop is closing next month.
It's a warm, truly spring-like day today.
Saying something like that isn't like her.

similar.title: 〜ようだ／〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: 〜ようだ is based on the speaker's own observations and feelings, so the judgment is more subjective; 〜らしい is mostly based on outside information and has a "secondhand" feel. 「熱があるようだ」 (I feel I have a fever), 「熱があるらしい」 (I hear they have a fever).

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: The hearsay 〜そうだ is a faithful report with a clear source; 〜らしい mixes in inference, so its reliability is vaguer.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: 「子どもっぽい」 means "childish (though not actually a child)", often negative; 「子どもらしい」 means "as a child should be", mostly positive.

meaning: 1) An inference based on the speaker's own observations or feelings ("it seems ..., it looks like ..."); 2) simile ("like ..."); 3) giving examples ("such as ..."). 〜みたいだ is the colloquial form of 〜ようだ.
connection: ようだ: plain form of verbs / i-adjectives, na-adjective + な, noun + の + ようだ; みたいだ: plain form of verbs / i-adjectives, na-adjective stem, noun + みたいだ
usage: Conjugates as a na-adjective: ような + noun, ように + verb, ようです, ようだった; likewise みたいな, みたいに, みたいです.
Differences in attachment: nouns 学生のようだ ↔ 学生みたいだ; na-adjectives 静かなようだ ↔ 静かみたいだ.
Similes often pair with まるで: 「まるで夢のようだ」, 「まるで子どもみたいに喜ぶ」.
Examples use ような／みたいな: 「東京のような大きな町」, 「りんごみたいな果物」.
〜ようだ is more written and formal; 〜みたいだ is more colloquial and casual and is not suitable for formal writing.
〜ように after a verb can also be "purpose" or 〜ようになる／〜ようにする, which are separate grammar points; this entry mainly covers forms like 「noun + のように」 and ようだ／ような.
scenarios: Inferring from signs: 「誰もいないようです。電気が消えています。」
Similes in descriptions (common in literature): 「雪のように白い肌。」
Casual speech among friends: 「あの二人、付き合ってるみたいだよ。」
Giving examples: 「パンダのような珍しい動物が見たい。」
etymology: 「よう」 is the kanji 「様」, meaning "appearance, state", and with the copula だ it means "it is the appearance of ...". 「みたい」 developed through contraction from 「〜を見たような」 → 「〜みたような」 → 「みたい」, and is generally thought to have settled in colloquial speech after the Meiji era; that is why it still attaches directly to nouns.
examples: It seems no one is here. The lights are off.
Her hands were as cold as ice.
I want to live in a big city like Tokyo.
I feel like I've met that person somewhere.
It's like something out of a dream, isn't it?

similar.title: 〜らしい
similar.explanation: 〜ようだ is based on the speaker's own observations, 〜らしい on outside information. Similes can only use 〜ようだ／みたいだ, not らしい (✕夢らしい话).

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: The appearance 〜そうだ is an intuitive impression of what's in front of you; 〜ようだ is an overall judgment. 「おいしそうだ」 = it looks delicious; 「おいしいようだ」 = it seems to be delicious (e.g. judging from how everyone is enjoying it).

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: In 「忘れないようにメモする」, ように expresses purpose and follows a verb; ように for similes is usually preceded by "noun + の".

meaning: Expresses a hypothetical condition: "if ..., then ...". It focuses on the first clause being a necessary condition for the second, and is also used for general rules, proverbs, and advice such as 〜ばいい (all you need to do is ...).
connection: Verb ba-form / conditional form (godan: 書く→書けば; ichidan: 食べる→食べれば; する→すれば; 来る→来れば); i-adjective: 高い→高ければ; na-adjective・noun: 静かなら(ば)／雨なら(ば)
usage: Formation: godan verbs change the final sound to the e-row + ば (行けば, 読めば, 話せば); ichidan verbs drop る and add れば (見れば); i-adjectives drop い and add ければ (安ければ); negative 〜ない→〜なければ.

The first clause is the condition and the second the result; the first clause is usually stative or conditional. When both clauses share a subject and the first has a volitional verb, the second generally can't be a command, request, or intention (✕早く行けば、席を取ってください) — use 〜たら instead.
Common set expressions: 〜ばいい (all you need to do is ... / it would be good to ...), 〜ばよかった (I wish I had ..., regret), 〜ば〜ほど (the more ..., the more ...).
Common in proverbs and general rules: 「春が来れば、花が咲く。」
Note that 〜ば is part of a conjugated form; the 「ば」 in 「てばかり」, 「例えば」, 「言葉」, etc. is not this grammar point.
scenarios: Giving advice: 「わからなければ、先生に聞けばいいですよ。」
Expressing regret: 「もっと勉強すればよかった。」
Explaining rules or conditions: 「この薬を飲めば、すぐ治ります。」
The more ..., the more ...: 「練習すればするほど上手になる。」
etymology: In Classical Japanese, "irrealis form + ば" expressed a hypothetical condition ("if ..."), while "realis form + ば" expressed a fixed condition ("because ..., since ..."). From the medieval period onward, realis + ば gradually took on the hypothetical meaning too, and the irrealis + ば use declined. So the modern "conditional (hypothetical) form" actually evolved from the classical "realis form" (已然形), which is why some grammar books still call it by that name.
examples: If you don't understand, just ask the teacher.
If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
I wish I had left earlier.
The more you practice Japanese, the better you get.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 〜たら has the widest range: its second clause can be a command, request, or intention, and it can also describe established facts ("when I did ..., I found ..."). 〜ば focuses on the condition itself, has restrictions on the second clause, and is common in writing and proverbs.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 〜なら takes up the listener's topic or assumes the first clause as a premise to give advice (「京都に行くなら、新幹線が便利だ」), and the time order of the two clauses can be reversed; 〜ば requires the first clause to happen before the second.

similar.title: 〜と
similar.explanation: 〜と expresses inevitable or habitual results (「春になると暖かくなる」), and its second clause cannot be an intention or request; 〜ば can also express general rules but puts more emphasis on the condition.

meaning: 1) Hypothetical condition: "if ..."; 2) definite condition: "when / once ..., (then)", doing the second action after the first is realized; 3) with a past-tense main clause, "when I ..., (I found that) ..."; 4) 〜たらどう？ makes a suggestion.
connection: Ta-form of verbs, adjectives, and nouns + ら (行ったら, 食べたら, 高かったら, 静かだったら, 雨だったら)
usage: Simple to form: just add ら to the past form ending in た／だ; the negative is 〜なかったら.
The most widely usable conditional: the second clause can be a command, request, intention, or invitation (「駅に着いたら、電話してください」).
It can express time sequence, "as soon as / once ...": 「家に帰ったら、すぐ宿題をします。」 Here the first clause is certain to happen and isn't a real hypothesis.
With a past-tense second clause, it expresses an unexpected discovery: 「窓を開けたら、雪が降っていた。」
Common uses: 〜たらいい (it would be good to ...), 〜たらどうですか (why don't you ...?, a suggestion), もし〜たら (if ...).
It is more colloquial than 〜ば; in formal situations you can use 〜ましたら (「わかりましたら、お知らせください」).
scenarios: Everyday arrangements: 「駅に着いたら、電話してね。」
Giving advice: 「疲れたら、少し休んだらどうですか。」
Describing an unexpected discovery: 「箱を開けたら、中は空だった。」
Expressing a hypothetical wish: 「もし宝くじが当たったら、世界旅行をしたい。」
etymology: 〜たら comes from 「たら」, the irrealis form of the Classical Japanese perfective auxiliary 「たり」, plus the conjunctive particle 「ば」, i.e. 「〜たらば」, meaning "if ... has happened". Later ば dropped off, leaving only 〜たら. The written form 「〜たらば」 can still occasionally be seen today.
examples: Please call me when you get to the station.
If it rains, the game will be canceled.
When I opened the window, it was snowing outside.
If you're tired, why don't you rest for a bit?
If they're cheap, I'd like to buy two.

similar.title: 〜ば
similar.explanation: 〜ば focuses on the condition, and its second clause shouldn't be an intention or request (when the first clause has a volitional verb); 〜たら has almost no restrictions, can also express time sequence and unexpected discoveries, and is more colloquial.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「東京へ行ったら、スカイツリーに登りたい」 is about after arriving in Tokyo; 「東京へ行くなら、新幹線がいい」 is advice before going. 〜なら allows the second action to happen before the first clause has taken place.

similar.title: 〜たあとで
similar.explanation: 〜たあとで only expresses simple time order; 〜たら includes the sense that the first clause is the trigger or condition.

meaning: 1) Takes up what the other person said or the current topic and uses it as a premise for advice, an opinion, or a judgment ("if (that's the case) ..., if it's ..."); 2) introduces a topic ("speaking of ..., as for ..."); 3) general hypothesis ("if ...").
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + なら; na-adjective stem / noun + なら (also written 〜ならば; colloquially 〜んなら／〜のなら)
usage: The most typical use is taking up the other person's topic to give advice: A「京都へ行きたいんです。」 B「京都へ行くなら、秋がいいですよ。」
The time order of the two clauses can be reversed: 「旅行に行くなら、カメラを買ったほうがいい」 (buy the camera first, then travel) — something 〜ば／〜たら can't do.
Noun + なら can introduce a topic, like "if it's ... you're asking about": 「田中さんなら、図書館にいますよ。」
In formal or emphatic speech say 〜ならば; in casual speech 〜のなら／〜んなら is common: 「行くんなら、早く行こう。」
Note that the なら in 「さようなら」, 「ならない」, 「並ぶ（ならぶ）」, and 「習う（ならう）」 is not this grammar point.
scenarios: Responding to what someone said with advice: 「パソコンを買うなら、この店が安いですよ。」
Introducing the topic to answer a question: 「鍵なら、机の上にありますよ。」
Expressing a conditional willingness: 「あなたが行くなら、私も行きます。」
Hypotheses in written language: 「もし事実ならば、大きな問題だ。」
etymology: 「なら」 is the irrealis form of the Classical Japanese copula 「なり」; with the conjunctive particle 「ば」 it forms 「ならば」, meaning "if it is ...". In modern colloquial speech ば is often dropped, giving 〜なら.
examples: If you're going to Kyoto, autumn is a good time.
If you're looking for Mr. Tanaka, he's in the library.
If you're going, I'll go too.
If that's really true, it's a serious matter.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 〜たら requires the first clause to be realized first; with 〜なら the second action can happen before the first clause is realized. 「お酒を飲んだら運転するな」 (Once you've had a drink, don't drive), 「お酒を飲むなら運転するな」 (If you're going to drink, don't drive).

similar.title: 〜ば
similar.explanation: 〜ば stresses the relationship between condition and result; 〜なら stresses advice and judgments "premised on what the other person said".

similar.title: 〜のなら／〜んなら
similar.explanation: Adding の puts more emphasis on "given that this is the situation", making the link to the previous statement clearer; very common in speech.

meaning: Passive voice: 1) direct passive, "be ...ed (by)" (the subject directly receives the action); 2) indirect passive / suffering passive (being troubled by someone else's action, "... happened (and it bothered me)"); 3) objective description with an inanimate subject (common in news and explanatory texts: 「この寺は500年前に建てられた」).
connection: Godan verbs: final sound to the a-row + れる (書く→書かれる, 言う→言われる); ichidan verbs: drop る + られる (食べる→食べられる, 見る→見られる); する→される; 来る→来（こ）られる
usage: The passive form conjugates as an ichidan verb: られた, られます, られて, られない. The agent is marked with 「に」 (母に叱られた); in writing, creators or makers often take 「によって」 (この絵はピカソによって描かれた).

The suffering passive can use intransitive verbs: 「雨に降られた」 (I got caught in the rain), 「子どもに泣かれた」 (the child cried, and I was at a loss). In English these are usually not translated with a passive at all.
Possessor passive: 「電車で足を踏まれた」 (someone stepped on my foot on the train); the subject is the person, and the affected body part or belonging takes 「を」.

Watch for overlapping forms: the passive of ichidan verbs and 来る is identical to the potential and honorific forms (食べられる = be eaten / can eat / eat (honorific)), and only context can tell them apart. This entry's patterns prioritize recall and will flag all of these identical forms, so judge by the meaning of the sentence.
「生まれる」, 「疲れる」, 「別れる」, 「慣れる」, 「流れる」, etc. are independent verbs, not passives. The patterns try to exclude their kana spellings, but occasional false hits are still possible.
scenarios: Describing what happened to you (often unpleasant): 「先生に叱られました。」
Objective description in news, reports, and explanatory texts: 「この橋は100年前に造られた。」
Expressing annoyance: 「隣の人にたばこを吸われて、困った。」
Passive expressions in academic and formal writing: 「この方法は広く使われている。」
etymology: The passive auxiliaries れる／られる come from Classical Japanese 「る／らる」. 「る・らる」 had four uses — spontaneous, potential, passive, and honorific — and their original core meaning is generally thought to have been "spontaneous" (something happening by itself), from which the other uses derived. This is the historical reason why the passive, potential, and honorific forms look the same in modern Japanese.
examples: When I was a child, I often got scolded by my mother.
Someone stepped on my foot on the train.
This temple was built 500 years ago.
I got caught in the rain on the way home and got soaked.
Japanese is studied all over the world.

similar.title: 〜せる・〜させる (causative)
similar.explanation: The causative means "make / let someone do"; the passive means "have something done to you". The two combine in the causative-passive 〜させられる, meaning "be made to do" (「母に野菜を食べさせられた」).

similar.title: Potential form 〜られる
similar.explanation: For ichidan verbs the potential and passive forms are identical: 「この魚は生で食べられる」 (can be eaten) vs. 「魚が猫に食べられた」 (was eaten). The godan potential is 書ける, 読める, different from the passive 書かれる, 読まれる; the colloquial "ra-less" forms (見れる, 来れる) are potential only.

similar.title: Honorific 〜れる・〜られる
similar.explanation: In 「先生が来られました」, られる is honorific (the teacher came), not passive. Check whether the subject is someone to be respected and whether there is an agent marked with 「に」.

meaning: Causative voice: 1) compulsion or command, "make (someone) do ..."; 2) permission or allowing, "let (someone) do ..., let (someone) do as they like"; 3) causing an emotion, "make (someone happy, worried, etc.)".
connection: Godan verbs: final sound to the a-row + せる (行く→行かせる, 読む→読ませる, 言う→言わせる); ichidan verbs: drop る + させる (食べる→食べさせる); する→させる; 来る→来（こ）させる
usage: The causative conjugates as an ichidan verb: させた, させます, させて, させない, させられる.
Particle for the person made to act: with intransitive verbs 「を」 is common (子どもを公園で遊ばせる); with transitive verbs use 「に」 (子どもに野菜を食べさせる), since there is already a 「を」.
The permission sense often appears as 〜させてあげる／〜させてやる; to ask permission for yourself, use 〜させてください／〜させていただけませんか (「今日は早く帰らせてください」).
The causative-passive 〜させられる means "be made to do": 「母に野菜を食べさせられた」; for godan verbs it is often contracted in speech to 〜される (行かされる, 待たされる), which is hard to tell apart from the passive.
Emotional causative: 「親を心配させる」, 「みんなを笑わせる」. The causative is generally not used directly toward superiors, as it may sound rude.
scenarios: Parents or teachers with children: 「子どもに毎日本を読ませています。」
Asking permission at work (a very common polite expression): 「この仕事、私にやらせてください。」
Describing being forced to do something: 「会議で長い時間待たせられた。」
Causing an emotion: 「そんなことを言って、母を悲しませてしまった。」
etymology: The causative auxiliaries せる／させる come from Classical Japanese 「す／さす」 (there was also 「しむ」). 「す」 attached to the irrealis form of yodan verbs and 「さす」 to other verbs, corresponding one-to-one with modern godan + せる and ichidan + させる. From the medieval period on, both shifted to shimo-ichidan conjugation and became 「せる・させる」. Classical 「す・さす」 also had an honorific use (as in 「せさせ給ふ」), which has disappeared in modern Japanese.
examples: The mother makes her child eat vegetables every day.
The teacher had the students write essays.
Excuse me, please let me rest for a bit.
His jokes always make everyone laugh.
Sorry for keeping you waiting so long.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (passive)
similar.explanation: The passive means "be ...ed"; the causative means "make / let ...". The causative-passive 〜させられる means "be forced to ...", with a sense of reluctance.

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: 〜てもらう means "have someone do something for you", with gratitude and a sense of a favor (「友だちに手伝ってもらった」); the causative is a command or permission from above, with no sense of a favor.

similar.title: Transitive verbs
similar.explanation: Some transitive/intransitive verb pairs are close in meaning to the causative: 「子どもを起こす」 (wake the child up, transitive) vs. 「子どもを起きさせる」 (make the child get up by themselves). The transitive verb means acting directly; the causative means having the other person do it themselves.

meaning: Expresses that the speaker (or the speaker's side) does something for someone else, giving them a favor ("do ... for someone"). Use 〜てさしあげる for superiors and 〜てやる for juniors, animals, and plants.
connection: Verb te-form + あげる (humble: 〜てさしあげる; toward inferiors: 〜てやる)
usage: The giver of the favor is the subject (usually the speaker or the speaker's side), and the recipient is marked with 「に」 or 「の」: 「妹に本を読んであげた」, 「友だちの宿題を手伝ってあげた」.
あげる conjugates as an ichidan verb: てあげた, てあげます, てあげよう, てあげたい, てあげて.
Saying 「〜てあげましょうか」 directly to an elder or superior sounds condescending, as if bestowing a favor; the polite way is 「お〜しましょうか」 (お持ちしましょうか).
〜てやる is used toward juniors, animals, and plants (「犬に餌をやる」, 「花に水をやる」), and can also mean "I'll show you" (in a defiant sense) (「絶対に勝ってやる」).
When the recipient is the speaker, 〜てあげる cannot be used; use 〜てくれる instead.
scenarios: Between friends and family: 「荷物、持ってあげるよ。」
Describing how you helped someone: 「道に迷った人に駅までの道を教えてあげました。」
Toward children or pets: 「子どもに絵本を読んでやる。」
Business or toward superiors (humble): 「お客様に資料をお送りしてさしあげました。」 (in actual business, お送りしました is more common)
etymology: あげる is written 「上げる」, originally meaning "to raise, to lift up". Lifting something up to offer it to a person of higher status gave rise to the meaning "to give". It was originally a humble word but gradually became neutral, meaning ordinary "give", so its original humble role was taken over by さしあげる (差し上げる).
examples: I read a book to my little sister.
That looks heavy. Let me carry it for you.
I showed a lost person the way to the station.
Every morning I take the dog for a walk.
I carried my teacher's bag for them.

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: 〜てくれる means someone else does something for "me (or my side)"; 〜てあげる means I do something for someone else. The directions are opposite.

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: 〜てもらう takes the recipient as subject: "I have / get someone to do it for me"; 〜てあげる takes the giver as subject.

similar.title: お〜する
similar.explanation: When offering help to an elder, the humble 「お持ちしましょうか」 is more appropriate than 「持ってあげましょうか」.

meaning: Expresses that someone else does something for the speaker (or the speaker's side), who benefits and feels grateful ("(someone) does ... for me"). Use 〜てくださる for superiors.
connection: Verb te-form + くれる (honorific: 〜てくださる)
usage: The giver of the favor is the subject (marked with が／は), and the recipient is the speaker or their "in-group", such as family; 「私に」 is usually omitted.
くれる conjugates as an ichidan verb (imperative くれ): てくれた, てくれます, てくれない？, てくれ.
〜てくれない？／〜てくれませんか is a common way to make a request, softer than 〜てください; 〜てくれ is a blunt command used mainly by men toward equals or juniors.
The masu-form of the honorific 〜てくださる is 〜てくださいます (not くださります), and the past is 〜てくださった／〜てくださいました.
It can't be used when the recipient isn't on the speaker's side: ✕「田中さんが山田さんに教えてくれた」 (between outsiders, use 〜てあげた).
scenarios: Expressing thanks: 「手伝ってくれて、ありがとう。」
Making a request: 「ちょっと窓を開けてくれない？」
Describing help you received: 「先生が丁寧に説明してくださいました。」
Complaining that someone doesn't help: 「夫は全然家事をしてくれない。」
etymology: くれる is written 「呉れる」; the old verb 「くる（呉る）」 meant "to give (to an inferior, to oneself)". From the medieval period on it was used specifically in the direction "someone gives to me", forming, together with あげる and もらう, Japanese's distinctive system of giving and receiving verbs. くださる is written 「下さる」, originally "to bestow (from above)", hence its honorific nature.
examples: My friend helped me move.
Thank you for coming.
Could you pass me the salt?
My teacher corrected my essay for me.
My mother always listens to me.

similar.title: 〜てあげる
similar.explanation: Opposite direction: 〜てあげる means I do something for others; 〜てくれる means others do something for me.

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: 「友だちが手伝ってくれた」 and 「友だちに手伝ってもらった」 describe the same fact; the former takes the giver as subject, the latter the recipient, and 〜てもらう can also imply "I asked for it".

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: 〜てください is a direct request; 〜てくれませんか／〜てくださいませんか are requests in question form, softer and more polite.

meaning: Expresses that the speaker (or their side) has someone do something for them, or benefits from someone's action ("have / get (someone) to do ... for me"). Use 〜ていただく for superiors.
connection: Verb te-form + もらう (humble: 〜ていただく)
usage: The recipient is the subject (usually "I"), and the giver is marked with 「に」 (sometimes 「から」): 「友だちに宿題を手伝ってもらった」.
もらう conjugates as a godan verb: てもらった, てもらいます, てもらえる, てもらいたい.
Requests: 〜てもらえませんか／〜ていただけませんか (could you please ...?) are very common, polite ways to ask.
〜てもらいたい／〜ていただきたい express wanting someone to do something and sound more formal than 〜てほしい.
It can express both actively asking (「医者に診てもらう」) and simply benefiting (「先生にほめてもらった」).
scenarios: Asking for help in daily life: 「友だちに写真を撮ってもらいました。」
Polite requests (common in business): 「すみません、もう一度説明していただけませんか。」
Going to a professional for treatment or repairs: 「病院で医者に診てもらった。」
Expressing a wish: 「この本をぜひ読んでもらいたい。」
etymology: もらう is written 「貰う」, originally meaning "to ask for and receive". いただく is written 「頂く／戴く」, originally "to place on top of one's head" — when receiving something from a person of higher status, one raised it above one's head out of respect — and so it became the humble word for "to receive" (the 「いただきます」 said before meals comes from this too).
examples: I had my friend help me move.
Excuse me, could you take a picture for me?
I had a doctor examine me at the hospital.
I had my teacher correct my essay.
I'd really like you to read this book.

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: For the same event, 〜てくれる takes the giver as subject and stresses that they did it for me of their own accord; 〜てもらう takes me as subject and can imply "I asked for it".

similar.title: 〜てあげる
similar.explanation: 〜てあげる means I do something for others; the direction of the favor is opposite to 〜てもらう.

similar.title: Causative 〜させる
similar.explanation: The causative is a command or permission from above; 〜てもらう is a request with gratitude toward the other person. 「子どもに掃除させる」 (make the child clean) and 「子どもに掃除してもらう」 (have the child kindly clean) differ greatly in tone.

meaning: Expresses contrast: the result is the opposite of what the first clause would lead you to expect, with the speaker's dissatisfaction, regret, surprise, or reproach ("even though ..., (still) ..."). At the end of a sentence it expresses regret or dissatisfaction ("if only ...", "... but oh well").
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + のに; na-adjective・noun + なのに
usage: Nouns and na-adjectives connect with な: 「日曜日なのに」, 「静かなのに」 (✕日曜日だのに).
The second clause is an established or definite fact; it cannot be a command, request, or intention: ✕「雨なのに、出かけてください」.
It carries strong emotion and is often used to express dissatisfaction or regret: 「せっかく作ったのに、誰も食べてくれない。」
Sentence-final uses: 「〜ばいいのに」 (it would be nice if ...), 「来ればよかったのに」 (you should have come).
Note there is also a purpose 「〜のに」 (「この箱は物を入れるのに便利だ」) unrelated to contrast; this entry's patterns try to exclude common combinations (のに便利・必要・使う, etc.).
scenarios: Expressing dissatisfaction: 「約束したのに、彼は来なかった。」
Expressing regret: 「もう少しで勝てたのに。」
Expressing surprise: 「もう4月なのに、まだ寒い。」
Reproach or regret (sentence-final): 「言ってくれればよかったのに。」
etymology: Made of the formal noun / nominalizing particle 「の」 + the case particle 「に」, originally meaning "in the situation of ...". From the early modern period onward it became fixed as a contrastive conjunctive particle expressing a result contrary to expectation and the speaker's dissatisfaction.
examples: He promised, but he didn't come.
Even though it's Sunday, I have to go to the office.
I studied so hard, but I still failed the exam.
It's already April, and it's still cold, isn't it?
You should have told me.

similar.title: 〜けれども／〜が
similar.explanation: 〜けど／〜が are neutral contrasts that just state the two clauses differ; 〜のに carries strong emotions such as dissatisfaction or surprise, and its second clause cannot be a request or intention.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to 〜のに, but written, more objective, and without strong personal emotion; common in news and essays.

similar.title: 〜ので
similar.explanation: 〜ので expresses a cause ("because ..., so"); 〜のに expresses contrast ("even though ..."). Be careful not to confuse them.

meaning: 1) Lists several parallel facts or reasons ("... and ..., and what's more ..."); 2) gives one or two reasons while implying there are others ("because ..., (and besides ...)").
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives / na-adjectives / nouns + し (noun・na-adjective: 〜だし); also after polite forms: 〜ですし, 〜ますし
usage: Common patterns: 「Aし、Bし、（それに）C」, 「Aし、Bから、〜」, used to list reasons or features.
Nouns and na-adjectives take だ: 「静かだし、便利だし」, 「雨だし」.
It can follow polite forms: 「この部屋は広いですし、駅にも近いです。」
The items listed usually point in the same evaluative direction (all advantages or all drawbacks); often paired with も: 「頭もいいし、性格もいい」.
Sentence-final use: 「だって、雨だし。」 means "well, (because) ..., you know", giving a soft reason or excuse in casual speech.
scenarios: Evaluating someone or something: 「彼は優しいし、頭もいい。」
Giving reasons or declining an invitation: 「今日は疲れたし、雨も降っているし、家にいます。」
Recommending: 「この店は安いし、おいしいし、おすすめですよ。」
Making excuses casually: 「別にいいじゃん、まだ時間あるし。」
etymology: The conjunctive particle 「し」 is generally thought to derive from 「し」, the attributive form of the Classical Japanese past auxiliary 「き」, or from the emphatic adverbial particle 「し」; from the early modern period it developed into a conjunctive particle for listing parallel items and reasons. There are several theories about its origin, and none is settled.
examples: This room is spacious and close to the station, so it's very convenient.
It's raining and cold today, so I don't want to go out.
He's kind, and he's a good cook too.
We don't have much time, so let's take a taxi.

similar.title: 〜から
similar.explanation: 〜から clearly states one reason; 〜し lists several reasons, or gives one while implying others, and sounds softer.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: 〜たり〜たり lists actions (as examples); 〜し lists facts, qualities, or reasons.

similar.title: 〜て／〜くて
similar.explanation: 「安くておいしい」 simply joins two qualities; 「安いし、おいしい」 stresses that "there's more than one reason" and often carries a judgment or evaluation.

meaning: Expresses that a degree exceeds the limit or appropriate range ("too ..., overly ..., over-..."), usually with a negative evaluation.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + すぎる; i-adjective (drop い) + すぎる (いい→よすぎる, ない→なさすぎる); na-adjective stem + すぎる
usage: すぎる conjugates as an ichidan verb: すぎた, すぎます, すぎて, すぎない.
Verbs: 「食べすぎる」, 「飲みすぎる」, 「働きすぎる」; adjectives: 「高すぎる」, 「静かすぎる」; negative ない→なさすぎる (自信がなさすぎる).
It can be nominalized as 〜すぎ: 「食べすぎに注意」, 「それは言いすぎだよ」.
It is generally negative, but in casual speech it is also used for exaggerated praise: 「かわいすぎる！」, 「おいしすぎる！」
Written 「過ぎる」 in kanji, but usually in kana as an auxiliary element; 過ぎ in 「10時過ぎ」 (past ten o'clock) refers to time and is not this grammar point.
scenarios: Commenting on prices while shopping: 「このかばんは高すぎて、買えません。」
Health warnings: 「お酒を飲みすぎないようにしてください。」
Reflecting on yourself: 「昨日は食べすぎた。」
Exaggerated praise in young people's speech: 「この猫、かわいすぎる！」
etymology: すぎる is written 「過ぎる」, originally meaning "to pass by, to go through (a place or time)". Going past a certain point means "exceeding" it, which extended to "going beyond the limit" in degree. In Classical Japanese it was the kami-nidan verb 「過ぐ」, which later became the kami-ichidan 「過ぎる」. (English "overdo" and "go too far" follow a similar logic.)
examples: I ate too much cake yesterday.
This bag is too expensive for me to buy.
This room is too quiet; it's a bit lonely.
Please don't drink too much.
That's going a bit too far.

similar.title: あまり〜ない
similar.explanation: 「あまり高くない」 means "not very expensive"; 「高すぎる」 means "too expensive (beyond what's acceptable)". The former is a low degree, the latter an excessive one.

similar.title: とても／すごく
similar.explanation: 「とても高い」 just means very expensive, not necessarily a problem; 「高すぎる」 clearly means it exceeds the limit and causes a problem.

similar.title: 〜にすぎない
similar.explanation: The N2 「〜にすぎない」 means "is nothing more than ...". Although it also uses すぎ, it expresses a low, negligible degree — the exact opposite of "excess".

meaning: 1) Doing something is easy or convenient ("easy to ..."); 2) something tends to happen easily ("apt to ..., prone to ...").
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + やすい
usage: Conjugates as an i-adjective: やすかった, やすくない, やすく（なる）, やすさ.
"Easy to do" is usually a positive evaluation: 「この本は字が大きくて読みやすい」, 「使いやすいパソコン」.
"Prone to happen" usually follows non-volitional verbs and is often negative: 「冬は風邪をひきやすい」, 「このガラスは割れやすい」.
Written 「〜易い」 in kanji but usually in kana; note it sounds the same as 「安い」 (cheap) but means something different.
The opposite is 〜にくい; in formal writing, "prone to (something bad)" can also be expressed with 〜がちだ.
scenarios: Reviewing products or tools: 「このペンはとても書きやすいです。」
Explaining precautions: 「雨の日は道がすべりやすいので、気をつけてください。」
Evaluating explanations or writing: 「先生の説明はわかりやすい。」
Describing someone's tendencies: 「彼は怒りやすい人だ。」
etymology: やすい is written 「易い」 and shares its origin with 「安い」; the old word 「やすし」 originally meant "calm, carefree, at ease". From "feeling at ease" it extended to "easy to do", and it became the second element of compound adjectives after the verb continuative form.
examples: This pen is very easy to write with.
The teacher's explanation was easy to understand.
It's easy to catch a cold in winter, so please be careful.
This glass breaks easily.

similar.title: 〜にくい
similar.explanation: Opposite: 〜にくい means "hard to ..., not easy to ...". 「読みやすい」 ↔ 「読みにくい」.

similar.title: 〜がちだ
similar.explanation: 〜がち means "tends to (often, something bad)", stressing frequency and tendency; 〜やすい stresses the quality of being "prone to". 「病気がちだ」 = often sick; 「病気になりやすい」 = easily gets sick.

similar.title: 〜やすい／安い
similar.explanation: 「安い（やすい）」 means "cheap" and is used as a standalone adjective; the やすい in this grammar point must follow a verb masu-stem.

meaning: Doing something is difficult or not easy, or something does not easily change ("hard to ..., difficult to ..., doesn't easily ...").
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + にくい
usage: Conjugates as an i-adjective: にくかった, にくくない, にくく（なる）, にくさ.
It can express the difficulty of an action (「この字は小さくて読みにくい」) or a quality that doesn't easily change (「割れにくいコップ」, 「燃えにくい素材」, often positive in this case).
It can express psychological difficulty: 「先生には言いにくい」, 「頼みにくい」.
Written 「〜難い（にくい）」 in kanji but usually in kana.
The near-synonym 〜づらい stresses that doing it is painful or uncomfortable (physically or mentally) and is common in speech; 〜がたい (N2) is written language meaning "(psychologically) hard to ...".
scenarios: Evaluating tools or products: 「この靴は歩きにくい。」
Finding it hard to bring something up: 「お金のことは、友だちには頼みにくい。」
Advertising a product's strengths: 「この服はしわになりにくい素材です。」
Commenting on writing or pronunciation: 「この言葉は発音しにくい。」
etymology: にくい is written 「憎い／難い」; the old word 「にくし」 originally meant "hateful, detestable". From "hateful to do" it extended to "hard to do", and as the second element of compound adjectives after the verb continuative form it expresses difficulty. Used on its own, 「憎い」 still keeps the meaning "hateful".
examples: These characters are small and hard to read.
This glass doesn't break easily.
There are some things that are a little hard to ask the teacher.
The new shoes were still hard to walk in.

similar.title: 〜やすい
similar.explanation: Opposite: 〜やすい "easy to ...". 「わかりやすい」 ↔ 「わかりにくい」.

similar.title: 〜づらい
similar.explanation: 〜づらい stresses that doing it is painful or uncomfortable (「足が痛くて歩きづらい」) and is mostly used for people's subjective feelings; for qualities of objects like 「割れにくい」, 割れづらい is generally not used.

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: 〜かねる (N2) means "(given one's position) cannot ...", a formal and polite way of declining (「お答えしかねます」); different from 〜にくい, which is about objective difficulty.

meaning: Expresses the speaker's intention or plan ("I think I'll ..., I'm going to ..."). 〜(よ)うと思っている expresses a plan held for some time.
connection: Verb volitional form + と思う (godan: 行く→行こう; ichidan: 食べる→食べよう; する→しよう; 来る→来（こ）よう)
usage: Forming the volitional: godan verbs change the final sound to the o-row + う (書こう, 読もう, 話そう, 買おう); ichidan verbs drop る + よう (見よう); する→しよう; 来る→来よう.
〜(よ)うと思う: a decision or idea at the moment of speaking; 〜(よ)うと思っている: a plan held for some time, which can also be used for a third person (「兄は留学しようと思っている」).
For the first person use 〜と思う, 〜と思います; a third person's plans are generally expressed with 〜と思っている or 〜つもりらしい.
The past 〜(よ)うと思った often means "I was going to ... (but didn't)": 「電話しようと思ったけど、忘れた。」
You can also say 〜(よ)うと考えている, which is more formal and sounds more carefully considered.
scenarios: Talking about weekend or holiday plans: 「週末は映画を見に行こうと思います。」
Talking about life plans: 「将来、日本で働こうと思っています。」
Explaining something you didn't get around to: 「昨日電話しようと思ったんですが、時間がなくて……。」
Announcing a resolution: 「今年こそ、たばこをやめようと思う。」
etymology: The volitional 〜(よ)う comes from the Classical Japanese conjectural auxiliary 「む」 (→ん→う), which expressed intention and conjecture; 「よう」 is the form 「う」 took after ichidan verbs. Classical 「〜むと思ふ」 already meant "I intend to ...", and modern 〜(よ)うと思う directly inherits this structure.
examples: I'm thinking of going to see a movie with friends this weekend.
I'm planning to study abroad in Japan next year.
I meant to call yesterday, but I forgot.
I think I'll go to bed early today.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: 〜つもりだ is a settled, fairly firm plan; 〜(よ)うと思う is often a fresh idea or a plan that may still change, and sounds softer.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: 〜たい only expresses a wish and doesn't necessarily lead to action; 〜(よ)うと思う expresses an intention to do it.

similar.title: 〜ようとする
similar.explanation: 〜ようとする means "be about to, try to" do something (「出かけようとしたとき、電話が鳴った」); it describes the moment just before an action or an attempt, not an inner plan.

meaning: Indicates the stage of an action in time: 1) dictionary form + ところだ: about to do ("be just about to ..."); 2) 〜ているところだ: in the middle of doing ("be in the middle of ...ing"); 3) ta-form + ところだ: just finished ("have just ..."); 4) 〜ところだった: almost ... (but didn't).
connection: Verb dictionary form / ている form / ta-form + ところだ
usage: Three stages: 「今から食べるところだ」 (about to eat) → 「今食べているところだ」 (eating right now) → 「今食べたところだ」 (just finished eating). Often used with 今から, ちょうど, 今, たった今, etc.
〜ところだった means "almost ... (but it didn't actually happen)", often with もう少しで: 「もう少しで遅刻するところだった。」
〜ところに／〜ところへ means "just as ... (someone came / something happened)": 「出かけようとしたところへ電話がかかってきた。」
〜ところを means "at the moment when ... (being seen, interrupted)": 「お忙しいところをすみません」.
「ところ」 originally means "place"; distinguish this from concrete noun uses such as 「住むところ」 (a place to live).
scenarios: Answering someone's question: 「今、ちょうど出かけるところです。」
Explaining what you're doing on the phone: 「今、ご飯を作っているところなんだ。」
Saying you've just finished: 「たった今、駅に着いたところです。」
A close call: 「もう少しで車にぶつかるところだった。」
etymology: 「ところ」 is written 「所」, originally meaning "place, location". From a "position" in space it extended to a "position, stage" in the progress of time, giving the uses "about to / in the middle of / just finished". As a formal noun it is usually written in kana. (Compare English "at this point" used for time.)
examples: I'm just about to go out.
I'm in the middle of making dinner right now.
I've just this moment arrived at the station.
I very nearly missed the train.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: 〜たところ refers to the moment just after completion in actual time; 〜たばかり means the speaker feels "not long ago" and can be used even after several months (「先月来たばかりです」), whereas ✕先月来たところです.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: 〜ている simply expresses an ongoing action; 〜ているところだ stresses "right in the middle of it at this very moment" and is often used to explain why you're busy now.

similar.title: 〜ようとする
similar.explanation: 〜ようとする means "try to, be about to", with a sense of intention; 〜るところだ objectively describes the stage in time.

meaning: Expresses that little time has passed since an action was completed ("have just ..."), focusing on the speaker's subjective feeling that the time is short.
connection: Verb ta-form + ばかりだ (colloquial: 〜たばっかり)
usage: Conjugates like a noun: たばかりだ, たばかりです, たばかりの + noun, たばかりなのに, たばかりで.
How long counts as "just" depends on the speaker's feeling: 「先月日本に来たばかりです」 (even a month later it still counts as "just arrived").
Often combined with 〜のに or 〜から: "even though I just ...", "since I just ...": 「買ったばかりなのに、壊れた。」
In speech 〜たばっかり is common; there is also 〜たてだ (焼きたて, できたて), meaning "freshly made", limited to a few verbs.
Distinguish it from 「〜てばかりいる」 (always ..., do nothing but ...), which follows the te-form and means something completely different.
scenarios: Introducing yourself: 「先週日本に来たばかりです。よろしくお願いします。」
Complaining: 「買ったばかりのパソコンがもう壊れた。」
Explaining your state: 「今起きたばかりで、まだ眠い。」
Explaining a lack of experience: 「入社したばかりなので、まだわからないことが多いです。」
etymology: 「ばかり」 comes from 「はかり」, the noun form of the verb 「計る（はかる）」 (to measure), originally meaning "estimate, approximate extent"; it later became voiced as the adverbial particle 「ばかり」, meaning "about, only, just". 〜たばかり thus means "only (that little time) since doing it", hence "have just done".
examples: I just came to Japan last week.
I lost the umbrella I had just bought.
I only just ate, but I'm already hungry.
Newborn babies are very small.

similar.title: 〜たところだ
similar.explanation: 〜たところ is the moment right after something ends in actual time; 〜たばかり is "not long ago" in a psychological sense, can cover a longer span, and can modify nouns (「買ったばかりの本」), while 〜たところ can't modify nouns this way to mean "just ...ed".

similar.title: 〜たあとで
similar.explanation: 〜たあとで only expresses order and says nothing about how much time passed; 〜たばかり stresses "very recently".

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: 「遊んでばかりいる」 means "always playing, doing nothing but play"; it follows the te-form and has nothing to do with "just".
